balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Airbus SE: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Airbus SE: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Airbus SE: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Airbus SE: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Airbus SE: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Airbus SE: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Airbus SE: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Airbus SE: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Airbus SE: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Airbus SE: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

airbusFcf.title: FCF before customer financing / company-defined FCF
airbusFcf.content:
FCF before customer financing is Airbus's own guided headline cash metric: free cash flow adjusted to exclude financing Airbus itself extends to airline customers to support aircraft deliveries. Free cash flow (company-defined) is Airbus's broader self-defined FCF measure (operating plus investing cash flows, adjusted for specific items it discloses separately), which differs from the generic Reported FCF = OCF - CapEx column shown elsewhere on this dashboard.

For Airbus SE: management guides the market on this measure every year, not on IFRS operating cash flow, and it is the number equity analysts quote against guidance. It swung to roughly -€7.5bn in FY2020 (COVID grounding) and back to the +€3-4.5bn range since -- a far bigger swing than the smoother net income line.

What to watch:

  • Delivery-rate shortfalls (A320/A350 supply chain) showing up here before they show up in revenue
  • Customer financing commitments building up off this adjusted measure
  • Recent periods may be blank: this figure is disclosed in Airbus's annual results press release/MD&A commentary, not always in the statutory financial statements file that gets extracted first

netCashPosition.title: Net cash position (Airbus-defined)
netCashPosition.content:
Net cash position is Airbus's own balance-sheet-strength measure: gross cash and cash equivalents plus short- and long-term securities, less gross financial debt, using Airbus's own scope (its FY2025 note discloses a gross cash position roughly double the net figure). This differs from the generic Cash vs Total Debt chart elsewhere on this dashboard, which uses the cross-ticker CashAndEquivalents/TotalDebt columns and does not include securities or Airbus's own debt scope.

For Airbus SE: this is the figure management and ratings agencies reference when discussing balance-sheet resilience through a production ramp or a downturn -- it fell from roughly €13.3bn (FY2017-2019) to €4.3bn in FY2020 during the COVID grounding, then rebuilt to €10.7bn by FY2023.

What to watch:

  • Net cash position trend relative to the generic cash/debt chart -- a persistent gap shows how much of reported cash sits in securities, not deposits
  • Rebuild speed after a shock, which is the balance sheet's main buffer against another production disruption
  • Recent periods may be blank pending extraction from the latest annual report's notes

aircraftOrders.title: Gross vs net aircraft orders
aircraftOrders.content:
Gross orders are new aircraft orders booked in the period before cancellations; net orders (already charted elsewhere) subtract cancellations from gross orders.

For Airbus SE: the gap between gross and net orders is the cancellation rate -- a leading indicator of airline customers' financial health and of confidence in Airbus's delivery schedule. Gross orders swung from 383 in FY2020 (COVID) to 2,319 in FY2023 as travel demand recovered.

What to watch:

  • A widening gross-to-net gap signalling rising cancellations
  • Order intake relative to the Backlog chart -- orders well below the annual delivery rate would start drawing the backlog down
